synopsis: Across the synthesis, machine-motion chapter and glossary, a fixed TTC threshold is judged a weak primary brake trigger at work-site speeds; ISO 21815-3:2023 instead uses stopping-distance and risk-zone logic, retaining TTC as an input or secondary layer for faster haul traffic [f148, f6202, f13894]. TTC becomes huge or unstable near zero closing speed, is undefined for a stationary machine starting up, and can miss articulation or track counter-rotation hazards; however, no head-to-head off-road comparison of distance-and-zone logic against TTC alone was found [f6214, f6219, f6218, f6224]. The proposed trigger distance combines detection/confirmation distance, travel during machine-action delay, stopping distance and safety clearance; braking zones must cover that distance, warning zones must add operator-reaction travel, and cited reaction assumptions range from 0.5–2.5 s [f13891, f13901, f13895]. Road benchmarks include the 2024 NHTSA NCAP setup with 12–40 m headways and 0.3–0.5 g target deceleration, while a 2026 simulation round robin used a 1.0 s TTC trigger explicitly as a research definition, not an earth-moving threshold [f2630, f6194]. No standard or peer-reviewed study supplies tuned off-road TTC or deceleration values, so program-specific models and tests must establish them; validation also needs recorded machine and actuator state to reconstruct TTC, zone entry and braking [f13885, f5663].

relations.note: Both reject fixed TTC as a strong primary trigger at work-site speeds.
Both favor stopping-distance and risk-zone formulation with TTC as one input.
Both identify missing published tuned off-road TTC and deceleration values.
